title: Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran — While US and Iran Talk Behind the Scenes
summary:
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump stood before the United Nations General Assembly in New York and laid out a stark choice: make a deal with Iran, or 'annihilate' the Islamic Republic.

'Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild... or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly?' Trump asked the standing-room-only crowd. Only one member of Iran's delegation watched.

But here's what makes the day unusual: even as Trump threatened overwhelming force, US and Iranian officials were actually communicating. Iran's Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, met with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff — not face to face, but through a Qatari mediator who shuttled between the two sides. Witkoff later posted on X that the talks 'successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive.'

Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, said Tehran's conditions include ending the war on all fronts and stopping US 'acts of aggression.'

This approach — threatening massive force while keeping negotiations open — is sometimes called coercive diplomacy. Trump has used it before, and he predicted a deal would come right after November's US midterm elections.

Trump also used his speech to reject 'global government,' promise to end Russia's war in Ukraine, and say the US must win the artificial intelligence race. He signed a deal with Denmark to expand the US military presence on Greenland.

The backdrop matters: the US-Israel war with Iran, which began in February, has pushed global oil prices up and dragged down Trump's approval ratings. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, speaking earlier, warned that global divisions are deepening.

So the world waits. Will there be a deal — or something much worse?
why_it_matters: Oil prices and the risk of a wider war reach straight into ordinary life — petrol, heating, food costs — and the way leaders mix threats with talks this year will shape how countries trust each other for a decade.

background_read: Donald Trump (the US president since 2025) has used this threat-and-offer style before: in his first term he pulled the United States out of a 2015 nuclear deal with Iran — an agreement in which Iran limited its nuclear program in exchange for the lifting of heavy economic sanctions — and replaced it with a 'maximum pressure' campaign.

The United Nations General Assembly (the yearly meeting in New York where leaders of nearly every country give speeches) has been used as a stage for exactly this kind of showdown for decades; John F. Kennedy used it in 1961 to challenge the Soviet Union in public.

Iran's government, formally called the Islamic Republic, is a theocracy, meaning religious leaders rather than voters hold the final say — which limits how far any negotiator can bend. Qatar (a small but very rich Gulf state) has become a regular go-between because it keeps open channels to both Washington and Tehran.

Analysts often point out that coercive diplomacy only works when the other side believes both the threat and the offer are real — and when it fails, it can push a country toward a weapons program instead of away from one.

perspectives.description: The striking thing is that talks are happening at all: a Qatari mediator is shuttling messages, Witkoff calls the round 'constructive', and Trump predicts a deal — proof that pressure and negotiation can work together.

Threatening to 'annihilate' a country in public could corner Iran's leaders, who may feel they cannot be seen to surrender. Instead of stopping a weapons program, humiliation and threats can convince a government that only nuclear weapons guarantee its survival.

Coercive diplomacy has a mixed record: it helped force changes in some standoffs but has also dragged countries into wars. It works only when the threat is credible and the offer is genuinely attractive — otherwise it becomes a countdown to conflict.

Everything now depends on what follows the US midterm elections and whether Washington can keep its regional allies and Iran at the table. If the channel through Qatar closes, the next headline may not be about a deal at all.
